title: Joseph of Arimathea (Mark 15:42–47)
hook: a council member boldly asks for the body and lays it in a tomb

segments.voice: Yesterday, a cry from the cross, the first line of Psalm 22, and your line was the women stayed. Did you stay with someone, even without words? Day two hundred twenty-eight.

When someone dies, somebody has to do the practical things. Call the family. Sign the forms. Pick the clothes. It's the least glamorous kindness there is, and often the bravest. It's late afternoon on Friday. Jesus is dead. The disciples are gone. The Sabbath begins at sunset, and in Jewish law a body shouldn't be left hanging overnight. Under Roman custom, the bodies of crucified rebels were often left on the cross, or thrown in a common grave. Somebody has to ask for him. And the man who does is someone we've never met before.
screen: `FRIDAY, LATE AFTERNOON.` → `THE SABBATH COMING AT SUNSET.` → `SOMEBODY HAS TO ASK.`

segments.voice: Mark introduces him in one breath, in the King James Bible: "Joseph of Arimathaea, an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God, came, and went in boldly unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus." Look at who he is. A counsellor: a member of the council, the same council that just condemned Jesus. Mark earlier said all of them condemned him; Luke adds that Joseph had not agreed with their decision. He's respected and he's comfortable. And he's waiting for the kingdom of God, which means he'd been listening. Then look at the verb. He went in boldly. The Greek word means he dared. Walking into the Roman governor's house to ask for the body of a man just executed as king of the Jews could cost him his standing, maybe more. He goes anyway. Pilate is surprised Jesus is already dead, calls the centurion to confirm it, and gives Joseph the body. Joseph buys fine linen, takes him down, wraps him, lays him in a tomb cut out of the rock, and rolls a stone against the door. And two people are watching: Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses. They see where he is laid. That detail matters for Sunday. Here's what's striking. The disciples, who knew him best, are nowhere. The one who shows up is a quiet insider who until now had kept his hopes to himself. Christians remember him as a patron of anyone who cares for the dead, and many churches honor him with a feast day. Sometimes courage is loud. Sometimes it's a respectable man asking an awkward question, and then doing the heavy lifting himself.
screen: `A COUNCILLOR, WAITING FOR THE KINGDOM.` · `HE DARED: HE WENT IN BOLDLY.` · `LINEN, ROCK AND A ROLLED STONE.` · `THE TWO MARYS SEE WHERE.` · then, large: `AND CRAVED THE BODY OF JESUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a brave kindness for someone gone. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has died: a grandparent, a friend, someone you barely knew. What's one kindness you could still do for them? Visit their grave. Call the person they left behind. Tell their story to someone who never met them. Pick the one that feels a little awkward, the one that takes a bit of daring. If you pray, you can remember them before God. The bell holds the time.
Joseph of Arimathea. The council member who dared to ask Pilate for the body of Jesus, and laid him in a tomb cut in the rock.
Your line: he went in boldly. Today, do the kindness that makes you a little nervous: the call, the visit, the question nobody else wants to ask. Day two hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: On Holy Saturday many churches keep a quiet day of waiting by the tomb; Orthodox Christians carry an embroidered cloth of the burial in procession, and Joseph of Arimathea is honored with a feast day in several churches.

fork.setup: you're a respected council member. the man you secretly hoped in has just been executed as a rebel king. the Sabbath is coming. what do you do?
options: go to Pilate and ask for the body.
fork.reveal: Joseph went in boldly to Pilate, craved the body, and buried Jesus himself in a rock tomb.

original.note: Greek: having dared. Mark 15:43, behind the King James "went in boldly".

trapdoor: what you thought: Joseph was just a rich man with a spare tomb.
what it means: a council member dared to ask Rome for the body of an executed man, risking his standing.
what a scholar hears: crucified bodies were often left unburied; the Sabbath and the law of Deuteronomy 21:23 add urgency.

sources.quoted: Joseph of Arimathaea, an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God, came, and went in boldly unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus.

notes: Roman practice of leaving crucified bodies unburied or in common graves: standard historical claim, though exceptions are attested; confirm phrasing 'often'.
Luke 23:51 says Joseph 'had not consented to the counsel and deed of them'; Mark 14:64 says 'they all condemned him'. Confirm the script's handling.
Joseph as patron of those who care for the dead (funeral directors, pallbearers): common attribution; confirm.
Feast days: Catholic (March 17 in some calendars), Orthodox (Sunday of the Myrrh-bearers), Anglican/Lutheran (July 31 or August 31). The script says only 'many churches'. Confirm.
Epitaphios procession on Holy Friday evening/Holy Saturday in Orthodox practice; howItsDone simplifies. Confirm.
